What was the purpose of the check-in?
As part of the adoption of the 2023-2026 strategic plan, staff made a commitment to check-in
at the midway mark to ensure that the plan remains responsive and adaptive to the rapidly
changing world around us, and also to ensure it stays aligned with our community's priorities.
This process allowed staff to evaluate progress on the implementation of the initial 30 actions,
identify emerging trends, opportunities and challenges that have emerged since the approval
of the plan, and determine if there are any gaps in our strategic plan that require additional
adjustments. In short, a check-in process helps us validate the continued relevance of the
plan and course correct where needed. By proactively responding to change and refining
our priorities, we reinforce our commitment to effective governance and ensure the strategic
plan remains a powerful tool for driving positive outcomes across the city.
Continuing the approach that was supported by Council during the development of the strategic
plan, the check-in process employed a strategic foresight lens to anticipate future needs
and ensure adaptability. Central questions that guided the check-in process included
how are we doing in implementing our first 30 actions, what has changed since the plan
was adopted in 2023, and are there emerging community needs or shifts in the operating
environment that we should be addressing now. The check-in process was shaped by a range
of engagement and research methods, including a community survey, stakeholder workshops,
expert consultations, public opinion polls, insights gathered from related strategic projects,
as well as Council interviews earlier this year.
In terms of progress, implementation of the strategic plan has maintained a disciplined
and phased approach.
We've seen strong momentum since the plan was adopted in 2023.
We are following a phased implementation approach with full maturity expected by the end of 2025,
meaning all projects will have started and or be completed or in progress by the end
2026 will be dedicated to completing existing work in a disciplined closeout phase with
no new projects added.
Two projects have been deprioritized and are being recommended for removal as part of this
check-in process, and I'll speak to that shortly in the presentation.
Overall, delays have been minimal in implementing our strategic plan actions, and we are now
reporting as of last fall on the majority of our strategic plan indicators, though performance
has been mixed.
We are still in the process of finalizing approximately 50% of our strategic plan targets,
so that remains a work in progress.
The key themes identified through expert insights, council interviews, public opinion polls,
internal and external workshops, and insights from related projects are summarized on the
screen, and they include economic growth, resiliency and prosperity, housing accessibility
and affordability, social resilience, public health and wellbeing, sustainable development
and responsible innovation. Notably, the economy and housing consistently ranked among the
top themes across all engagement and research methods, while other themes appeared prominently
in several areas, but not all sources.
I do want to clarify that these six top themes should not be read as a new set of strategic
priorities for the city.
Rather, there is strong alignment between the top themes that we heard through this
check-in process and the city's current strategic plan, reinforcing the relevance and responsiveness
of the plan. As presented in the report, the insights and feedback from the check-in process
strongly affirm that we are on the right track. There's clear alignment between the community's
current priorities and the initiatives already underway in the strategic plan. In fact, 23
current strategic plan initiatives are advancing shared goals across the themes that we heard
about during the check-in process. While most challenges and opportunities align with ongoing
priorities, a gap analysis revealed that a few emerging or evolving areas have surfaced
as key considerations for the city. This has resulted in a series of proposed adjustments
to the strategic plan, as well as several recommended actions that fall outside of the
plan. And that's what I'll share with you now. So two initiatives are recommended for
deprioritization and removal due to limited funding, resource constraints and reallocation
of staff resources, as well as more time needed to assess evolving community needs after the
Kitchener Indoor Recreation Complex has opened next year. And these two projects being recommended
for removal of the current plan include the Sport and Recreation Master Plan and the Recreation
and Leisure Program Review. These projects will be reconsidered for possible inclusion
in the 2027-2030 strategic plan. Two initiatives are being recommended for addition to the
current strategic plan to sharpen the City's focus on economic resiliency, reflecting both
Council's feedback and community priorities. This includes a Make It Kitchener 2.0 scoped
refresh and the Downtown Safety and Security Action Plan implementation.
Finally, additional actions are being recommended outside of strategic plan actions or initiatives,
and these include improving the communication on the progress towards our strategic plan
goals through the addition of new strategic plan indicators that tell a more outcome-focused
story. Further exploring the theme of social resilience to understand if there's a
pressing service delivery opportunity within this theme area will also occur. This came
up several times throughout the check-in process. And with a lens on efficient and effective
Service delivery, we are adjusting the scope of the Digital Kitchener strategy to both leverage AI
and prioritize innovation lab projects that drive cost-effective service delivery.
In 2026, we're also expanding the City's Lean training program for up to 50 more
managers across the City to help with service efficiency and delivery.
And lastly, we're exploring collaborations actively with academic institutions to conduct
research on community organizations that are operating in the space of our strategic plan
priorities, aiming to uncover collaboration and or knowledge sharing opportunities.
So in conclusion, the check-in process affirms that the plan strength, sorry, that the plan
is still strong and relevant while recommending several targeted improvements or refinements.
The insights gathered provide momentum and direction for the 2027 to 2030 strategic planning
cycle, which will begin early next year.
This check-in process reinforces that refinement of the current plan, not reinvention, is likely
an appropriate path forward.
